# The Elements

::: {.callout-question}

When a system cannot maximize every property at once, which ones decide the
design?

:::

A placement that looks right on a spec sheet can still fail in the room, and
usually for the one reason nobody measured. The detector fit in memory, the model
was accurate enough, the power draw was within budget, and the robot still turned
its head half a second late, every time. Something in the loop was over its
budget. From the outside, there was no way to tell which.

That scene fails for want of two things. One is a way to judge a design that does
not let any single budget hide: the properties a physical AI system is held to,
and the rule that it must satisfy all of them at once. The other is the means to
see those budgets at all, because a constraint you cannot measure is one you
discover the hard way.

## What a system is judged by

A system is built from components, perception, cognition, action, memory, and
learning, but it is judged by its properties. The nine below are the vocabulary
the rest of the book uses, and [placement](07-placement-and-systems.qmd) is the
act of trading them against one another.

| Element | What it means | Where it bites hardest | How you measure it |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Timeliness** | the world has deadlines; late is wrong | control, perception | end-to-end latency, deadline misses |
| **Reliability** | runs unattended; failure is physical | action, deployment | time between failures, recovery time |
| **Safety** | actions can harm; fail-safe is mandatory | action | bounded motion, time to safe stop |
| **Memory and state** | persists and accumulates; not stateless | memory, learning | recall accuracy, state growth |
| **Energy and thermal** | embodied means power-bound | perception, on-device models | joules per task (energy), milliwatts (power), temperature |
| **Privacy and trust** | senses private spaces | sensing, data, deployment | data egress, on-device retention |
| **Robustness** | the open world is out of distribution | perception, cognition | degradation under shift, failure modes |
| **Adaptivity** | improves from its own experience | learning | data yield, improvement per cycle |
| **Observability** | you can explain what it did and why | cognition, deployment | traceability of a decision |

## The budget identity

The properties are not a wish list you score and total. They are budgets, and a
capability fits a given placement only if every budget closes at once. Four of
them carry hard numeric ceilings, latency, memory, energy, and bandwidth, and
together they make the chapter's iron law:

$$\text{fits} \iff \max_{b}\ \frac{\text{used}_b}{\text{limit}_b}\ \le\ 1$$

In words: latency under the deadline, and memory under the limit, and energy
under the budget, and bandwidth under the link, all at the same time. Averaging
does not help; three budgets with room to spare do not buy back the one that is
over. The budget with the highest ratio of used to limit is the **binding
constraint**, the single property that decides the placement. @fig-budget-fit
shows a capability that misses on exactly one.

::: {#fig-budget-fit fig-cap="**The budget identity**: a capability fits a placement only if every budget closes; here three have headroom and latency is over its limit, so latency is the binding constraint and the placement does not fit." fig-alt="Four horizontal bars labeled latency, memory, energy, and bandwidth, each showing used divided by limit against a dashed vertical limit line. Memory, energy, and bandwidth end before the line; latency extends past it and is labeled the binding constraint."}
![](../assets/diagrams/budget-fit.svg)
:::

Naming the binding constraint is the move you make in every chapter. It turns
"this feels too slow" into "latency is over by fifteen percent and nothing else
is close," which is something you can act on: relax the deadline, cut the work, or
move the capability to a different box. The other five properties, reliability,
safety, privacy, robustness, and adaptivity, are no less real, but they act as
constraints and postures rather than simple ceilings, so they shape the placement
without entering the same arithmetic.

## The three that bind first

Nine properties are too many to hold at once on a first build, and you do not
have to. For any given system a few dominate and the rest follow. The decision
this chapter asks of you is to name the three that bind first, rank them, and
defend the ranking by which budgets are tightest. For a robot in a child's room a
defensible three is timeliness, safety, and privacy: the loop has deadlines, the
body can do harm, and the room is private. A warehouse arm behind a cage would
rank them differently, with safety and reliability ahead of privacy. The point is
not the particular list. It is that you can say which three, and why, before you
write any code.

## You cannot budget what you cannot see

All of this assumes you can measure the budgets, which is why observability is the
property you build first, not last. In an open loop you can read the output and
check it at your leisure. In a closed loop the evidence is gone by the next cycle,
so the only way to know which budget binds is to instrument the loop and watch the
terms go past. Observability here is not logging for its own sake; it is the
precondition for every other decision in this book. Build it once and you reuse it
in every chapter.

::: {.callout-build title="Make the budgets visible"}

Take the simplest loop you can run, sense then act, on any board or your laptop.
Around it, log the four budget terms every cycle: the time each stage takes, the
memory in use, the energy if your board reports it, and the bytes moved on any
link. Show each as a ratio of used to its limit, and read off the binding
constraint.

On the kit later, the same harness spans the UNO Q's two brains, the Linux SoC
and the real-time MCU, over a shared-memory ring buffer, and every later lab plugs
into it. If your board cannot report energy or bandwidth, log latency and memory,
the two you can always get, and reason about the rest. Either way you leave with a
loop you can see into and the binding constraint named.

:::

## Read

The shape of the budget identity is the roofline model from computer architecture
(Williams, Waterman, and Patterson, 2009), which bounds performance by whichever
resource saturates first and draws the rest as headroom under a ceiling. The
binding constraint is that saturating resource. Finding it before optimizing
anything is among the oldest habits in systems work; physical AI asks you to apply
it not to one resource but to a budget of nine properties at once.

::: {.callout-teaching}

- **Hook**: hand students the empty table and the robot, and have them fill in
  "how you measure it" from their own build before reading the chapters. The
  column they cannot fill is the property they have no way to see yet.
- **Open question**: nine properties may be too many to meet at once. Which three
  are the irreducible core for a first pass? Candidates: timeliness, safety,
  privacy.
- **Watch**: keep the budget identity from reading as "optimize everything." The
  lesson is the opposite: find the one budget that binds, and spend your effort
  there.

:::
